newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil to use AZT to stop HIV infection in babies.
newsitem.headline: Brazil to use AZT to stop HIV infection in babies.

text.p: Brazil's Health Ministry has authorized the use of the AZT anti-viral drug to help stop the transfer of the HIV infection from mothers to babies, a spokesman for Brazil's anti-AIDS program said on Monday.

The spokesman said Health Minister Carlos Alburquerque authorized the allocation of funds to the project after French and U.S. tests showed a marked decrease in the transmission of the virus if women are treated with AZT during childbirth.

"The results prove the strong impact that the use of AZT can have in reducing the vertical transmission of HIV (from mother to baby)," said Pedro Chequer, coordinator of the government's anti-AIDS campaign.

"Naturally, they also reveal the unarguable reduction in social costs that will result from the considerable drop in the number of orphaned children infected with AIDS," he added in a news sheet distributed by the anti-Aids campaign.
The news sheet said that an international study of the application of AZT during pregnancy and child birth showed clear results.
It said that in a control group of 184 babies and mothers given placebos during pregnancy and birth HIV was carried over to 25.5 percent of the newborn.
In a group of 180 babies treated with AZT, only 8.3 percent were infected with HIV.
The studies concluded that the injection of AZT during childbirth was particularly significant in reducing the transmission of the virus that causes AIDS, the ministry said.

Brazil suffers one of the world's highest incidences of AIDS with an estimated 95,000 cases of HIV infection registered. But health officials estimate as many as 450,000 out of Brazil's 160 million people may be carrying the virus.
